correctness.rationale: In total degrees at most p, all on-leading-degree binomial coefficients are nonzero, and the first n−hd columns of the h-th power (when positive) give all pivots, so both ranks are max(n−hd,0). At n=p+1 the only surviving product into the last coordinate is e1∘ep. Writing right multiplication as the p-dimensional truncated operator T plus the final-coordinate row a_p e1*, that row does not increase the first-power rank for d≤p−1: the first column has a unique leading pivot and all columns beyond p−d vanish. In higher powers the correction vanishes because e1* T=0. The row alone gives a single length-two chain when d=p. For the left operator, d=1 has nonzero consecutive pivots through e_{p+1}; for d≥2 there is no last-coordinate output at all. This proves all the stated power ranks (including p=2) and thus the Jordan table over any ground field of characteristic p. Counting the first nonzero coordinates gives the displayed census and rank strata, including the q vectors with only the last coordinate possibly nonzero; the annihilator statements follow from the zero ranks. A fresh explicit-matrix computation independently checked the positive-power ranks on seven exhaustive configurations, including F4 and (p,q,n)=(5,5,6), whose joint multiplicities matched the stated 5,20,100,500,2500,12500.
residual_risks: Finite tests corroborate; the triangular proof establishes the infinite family. No assertion beyond n=p+1 or about nonreduced rank schemes is validated.

value.rationale: This identifies the precise first dimension where division-free binomial structure changes handed multiplication, and distinguishes a missing left rank, the exceptional last-coordinate action, and the complete joint strata. The uniform all-element type table is a natural invariant and informs both finite-field and arbitrary-field questions; counting examples only at p=2 would not supply this value.
residual_risks: The useful result is a low-dimensional boundary classification, not an all-dimensional Zinbiel classification.
